section.title: Elihu's Fourth Speech
section.sectionRationale: Elihu's final and longest speech begins with one more defense of God's justice and disciplining purposes in affliction, then rises into an extended, awestruck description of a coming thunderstorm, rain, snow, lightning, wind, all obeying God's command without needing anyone's understanding of how. This nature hymn builds and builds until it nearly becomes the LORD's own voice; by the time God actually speaks from the whirlwind in chapter 38, the storm Elihu has been describing seems to have arrived.
section.thesis: Elihu closes his case not with a new argument but with wonder, God's mastery over rain, snow, lightning, and thunder is beyond human understanding or control, and this note of awe, more than any of Elihu's arguments, is what actually prepares Job, and the reader, for the LORD's own appearance.
section.frameNote: Two chapters, seven movements: Elihu's claim to bring perfect knowledge; God's justice toward the afflicted, using affliction to open their ears; a warning against turning toward iniquity under pressure; God's greatness displayed in the gathering storm; the obedient elements, thunder, lightning, snow, and rain; a call to stand still and consider God's wonders; and a closing confession that the Almighty is beyond our reach.

units.label: One perfect in knowledge
units.note: Elihu's claim to speak for God

verses.text: And Elihu continued:
“Bear with me a little longer, and I will show you that there is more to be said on God’s behalf.
I get my knowledge from afar, and I will ascribe justice to my Maker.
For truly my words are free of falsehood; one perfect in knowledge is with you.

units.label: Justice toward the afflicted
units.note: He opens their ears through suffering

verses.text: Indeed, God is mighty, but He despises no one; He is mighty in strength of understanding.
He does not keep the wicked alive, but He grants justice to the afflicted.
He does not take His eyes off the righteous, but He enthrones them with kings and exalts them forever.
And if men are bound with chains, caught in cords of affliction,
then He tells them their deeds and how arrogantly they have transgressed.
He opens their ears to correction and commands that they turn from iniquity.
If they obey and serve Him, then they end their days in prosperity and their years in happiness.
But if they do not obey, then they perish by the sword and die without knowledge.
The godless in heart harbor resentment; even when He binds them, they do not cry for help.
They die in their youth, among the male shrine prostitutes.
God rescues the afflicted by their affliction and opens their ears in oppression.

units.label: A warning against turning to iniquity
units.note: do not long for the night

verses.text: Indeed, He drew you from the jaws of distress to a spacious and broad place, to a table full of richness.
But now you are laden with the judgment due the wicked; judgment and justice have seized you.
Be careful that no one lures you with riches; do not let a large bribe lead you astray.
Can your wealth or all your mighty effort keep you from distress?
Do not long for the night, when people vanish from their homes.
Be careful not to turn to iniquity, for this you have preferred to affliction.

units.label: God's greatness in the gathering storm

verses.text: Behold, God is exalted in His power. Who is a teacher like Him?
Who has appointed His way for Him, or told Him, ‘You have done wrong’?
Remember to magnify His work, which men have praised in song.
All mankind has seen it; men behold it from afar.
Indeed, God is {{gadol|great}}, beyond our knowledge; the number of His years is unsearchable.
For He draws up drops of water which distill the rain from the mist,
which the clouds pour out and shower abundantly on mankind.
Furthermore, who can understand how the clouds spread out, how the thunder roars from His pavilion?
See how He scatters His lightning around Him and covers the depths of the sea.
For by these He judges the nations and provides food in abundance.
He fills His hands with lightning and commands it to strike its mark.
The thunder declares His presence; even the cattle regard the rising storm.

units.label: Thunder, lightning, snow, and rain obey
units.note: so that all men may know His work

verses.text: “At this my heart also pounds and leaps from its place.
Listen closely to the thunder of His voice and the rumbling that comes from His mouth.
He unleashes His lightning beneath the whole sky and sends it to the ends of the earth.
Then there comes a roaring sound; He thunders with His majestic voice. He does not restrain the lightning when His voice resounds.
God thunders wondrously with His voice; He does great things we cannot comprehend.
For He says to the snow, ‘Fall on the earth,’ and to the gentle rain, ‘Pour out a mighty downpour.’
He seals up the hand of every man, so that all men may know His work.
The wild animals enter their lairs; they settle down in their dens.
The tempest comes from its chamber, and the cold from the driving north winds.
By the breath of God the ice is formed and the watery expanses are frozen.
He loads the clouds with moisture; He scatters His lightning through them.
They swirl about, whirling at His direction, accomplishing all that He commands over the face of all the earth.
Whether for punishment or for His land, He accomplishes this in His {{chesed|loving devotion}}.
Listen to this, O Job; stand still and consider the {{niphlaot|wonders}} of God.
Do you know how God dispatches the clouds or makes the lightning flash?
Do you understand how the clouds float, those wonders of Him who is perfect in knowledge?
You whose clothes get hot when the land lies hushed under the south wind,
can you, like Him, spread out the skies to reflect the heat like a mirror of bronze?
Teach us what we should say to Him; we cannot draw up our case when our faces are in darkness.
Should He be told that I want to speak? Would a man ask to be swallowed up?

units.label: The Almighty is beyond our reach

verses.text: Now no one can gaze at the sun when it is bright in the skies after the wind has swept them clean.
Out of the north He comes in golden splendor; awesome majesty surrounds Him.
The Almighty is beyond our reach; He is exalted in power! In His justice and great righteousness He does not oppress.
Therefore, men {{yirah|fear}} Him, for He is not partial to the wise in heart.”

gadol.gloss: Great, large, vast. Elihu declares God gadol, great, beyond our knowledge, a claim his own nature poem then illustrates at length through the incomprehensible mechanics of rain, thunder, and lightning.

chesed.gloss: Loving devotion, steadfast covenant love, kindness. Elihu says God sends storms, whether for punishment or for blessing His land, in chesed, His own faithful, loving purpose, tying even the terrifying power of weather to God's covenant character.

niphlaot.gloss: Wonders, marvelous or extraordinary works, from the root pala, to be surpassing or beyond ordinary capacity. Elihu commands Job to 'stand still and consider the wonders of God,' the same word used throughout the Psalms for God's mighty and awe inspiring deeds.

yirah.gloss: Fear, reverence, awe. Elihu's closing conclusion, that all people fear God because of His inaccessible greatness and unyielding justice, sets the emotional and theological stage exactly where God's own speech from the whirlwind will begin in the next chapter.

basic.context: Elihu's final speech opens with one more claim to bring God's own perspective, then defends God's justice and disciplining purposes in suffering. But the speech's real power is in its second half, an extended, breathless description of a gathering thunderstorm, rain, snow, lightning, and wind, all obeying God without human understanding of how. By its end, the storm Elihu describes seems to have actually arrived, setting up God's appearance from the whirlwind in the very next chapter.
basic.hermeneutics: This speech functions as a hinge in the book: Elihu's arguments about justice largely repeat his earlier points, but his nature poetry does something new, it shifts the register from argument to awe, from explaining suffering to marveling at incomprehensible power. This shift prepares both Job and the reader for God's own speech, which will use exactly this kind of creation imagery rather than legal argument.
basic.originalLanguages: Elihu declares God gadol, great, beyond comprehension, and describes storms sent in chesed, His steadfast, loving purpose, whether for judgment or blessing. He calls Job to consider God's niphlaot, wonders, and concludes that all people rightly hold yirah, reverent fear, before such inaccessible majesty, the exact note God's own voice will strike beginning in chapter 38.
basic.typology: Elihu's storm, God's voice thundering, lightning obeying His command, anticipates the LORD's own appearance out of the whirlwind in the next chapter, and further anticipates the New Testament's pattern of divine appearances in storm and glory, culminating in Christ's authority over wind and waves, Mark 4:39-41.
basic.christ: Elihu marvels that no one can command the lightning or instruct the clouds, questions that find their startling answer in the Gospels, where the disciples ask in amazement, 'Who is this, that even the wind and the waves obey Him?' Mark 4:41, discovering in Jesus the very authority over creation that Elihu says belongs to God alone.
basic.god: God's power over weather is here presented not as arbitrary force but as chesed, loving devotion, purposeful whether in judgment or blessing; this same God is about to speak directly to Job, and Elihu's closing note of reverent fear rightly prepares the reader for that encounter.
basic.crossReferences: Psalm 29 similarly pictures the LORD's voice in the thunder over the waters. Mark 4:39-41 has Jesus command the wind and sea, provoking the same awe Elihu describes. Psalm 147:8, 16-18 credits God with controlling rain, snow, and frost. Nahum 1:3 describes the LORD's way in the whirlwind and storm.
basic.oneStory: Elihu's closing speech moves from argument to awe, describing a God whose command over thunder, lightning, snow, and rain leaves humanity in reverent fear. This same authority over creation is claimed and displayed by Jesus Christ, who commands wind and waves with a word, revealing that the God Elihu describes from a distance has drawn near in a person.

context.literary:
This is the longest of Elihu's speeches and the last human voice in the book before the LORD speaks. It falls into four parts. Job 36:1-4 is a preface in which Elihu asks for patience and makes his boldest claim, "one perfect in knowledge is with you." Job 36:5-21 is a teaching about how God deals with the afflicted, first in general terms, then in warning to Job by name. Job 36:22-37:13 is a hymn, opening with "God is exalted in His power" and moving through rain, thunder, lightning, snow, ice and wind. Job 37:14-24 turns back to Job with a run of questions and ends with a confession of human helplessness and a call to fear.

The middle of the speech is a hinge between two registers. Before Job 36:22 Elihu argues. After it, he mostly describes. The language changes from cause and effect, deed and reward, to things seen: drops drawn from the sea, clouds spread like a canopy, lightning gathered in the hands of God. The change is not a break in thought, since Elihu says the same weather that judges nations also feeds them, Job 36:31, and that God sends it whether for punishment, for His land or in loving devotion, Job 37:13.

Two lines frame the speech and read like a small irony. In Job 36:4 Elihu says of himself that one "perfect in knowledge" is with Job. In Job 37:16 he describes God as the one "perfect in knowledge" and asks whether Job understands His wonders. The same description is claimed by the speaker and then by the God he is describing. Whether Elihu meant the echo or not, the reader hears it.

The speech ends without a conclusion. Job 37:24 stops on the fear of God, and Job 38:1 says, "Then the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind." Elihu's storm and God's storm meet, and Elihu is not mentioned again.
context.historical:
Elihu describes weather with the eye of someone who lives by it. Rain and snow decided the harvest, the flocks and the roads, and the coming of a storm sent animals to their dens, Job 37:8. The description of water drawn up as mist and poured out as rain, Job 36:27-28, shows a good grasp of the water cycle as it could be observed, and it stands with other biblical remarks: Amos 5:8 speaks of the One who summons the waters of the sea and pours them over the face of the earth, and Psalm 135:7 says that He causes the clouds to rise from the ends of the earth.

The thunderstorm was also the standard setting for meeting God. At Sinai the people saw thunder and lightning and a mountain wrapped in smoke, and they trembled and said, "do not let God speak to us, or we will die," Exodus 20:18-19. Psalm 18:9-15 describes the LORD coming down with dark clouds beneath His feet, thundering from heaven, shooting arrows of lightning. Psalm 29 repeats "the voice of the LORD" seven times. A hearer in Elihu's world would take a storm as a visible sign of God's voice, and the speech invites Job to hear it that way.

The reference in Job 36:14 to death "among the male shrine prostitutes" points to the cult of Canaan and its neighbours, and it is meant to say that the godless die in shame and early. The man who is "laden with the judgment due the wicked" in Job 36:17 has to be read in the light of Elihu's argument, not in the light of the prologue.

The remark that a man's clothes get hot "when the land lies hushed under the south wind," Job 37:17, is the sort of thing said by someone who knows the hot wind of the desert, and the "mirror of bronze" for the sky, Job 37:18, is a precise image from a world where mirrors were polished metal, not glass.
context.canonical:
Elihu's hymn of the storm sits within a long line of biblical poems where God is met in wind, cloud and thunder. Psalm 29 says, "The voice of the LORD is over the waters; the God of glory thunders." Psalm 18:13 says, "The LORD thundered from heaven." Psalm 147:15-18 describes the LORD sending His word to the earth, spreading snow like wool and scattering frost like ashes, and then sending His word to melt it. Isaiah 55:10-11 uses the fall of rain and snow as a picture of how God's word does not return empty. Job 37:6 belongs with these, where God says to the snow, "Fall on the earth."

The link to what follows in Job is immediate. God's speech in chapters 38 and 39 takes up almost every item from Elihu's list. Job 38:22 asks whether Job has entered the storehouses of snow, and Job 38:34-35 asks whether he can command the clouds or send the lightning bolts on their way. Elihu asked, "Do you know how God dispatches the clouds or makes the lightning flash?" Job 37:15. The LORD then asks the same questions in His own voice, and He does not mention Elihu. Ezekiel 1:4 opens the prophet's vision of glory with a whirlwind coming from the north, a great cloud with fire flashing, which is how Elihu says God comes in Job 37:22.

The New Testament carries the theme in two ways. Jesus stills a storm on the Sea of Galilee and the disciples ask, "Who is this, that even the wind and the sea obey Him?" Mark 4:41. And Paul closes his great argument about God's ways with, "O, the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are His judgments," Romans 11:33, which is Elihu's conclusion in Job 36:26 and 37:23 applied to redemption.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The writer places Elihu's last words in front of the LORD's first ones so that the book's turn from argument to wonder does not come as a shock. Elihu spends much of chapter 36 on the old subject, that God punishes the wicked, rescues the afflicted and pulls the repentant back from the edge, Job 36:5-15. Then he warns Job, Job 36:16-21, and finally he abandons argument for the storm. By the end he is confessing what none of the earlier speakers admitted: "The Almighty is beyond our reach," Job 37:23, and "we cannot draw up our case when our faces are in darkness," Job 37:19.

The writer wants readers to feel two things. First, that the wonders of creation do not fit into any human system of explanation, however clever, and that a person who stands before them is quiet. Second, that Elihu's own words are caught by his own conclusion. He says no one can teach God what to say, Job 37:19, and no one can tell Him that he wants to speak, Job 37:20, yet he has just spent six chapters doing exactly that. The tension is left for the reader to resolve, and it is resolved when the LORD speaks.

The first hearers were meant to leave the speech with the sense of a storm about to break. What Elihu began as a hymn becomes a kind of overture.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The nature poetry of Job 36:27-37:13 describes what Elihu sees and what he draws from it. It is not a scientific manual, and it does not command us to read weather as a message about anyone's guilt. Elihu himself says that the same storm may be for punishment, for His land or for loving devotion, Job 37:13, and in that phrase he refuses the idea that we can look at a storm and know its purpose. That is a useful correction to his own earlier claims about Job.

What applies is the posture the hymn commends. Job 37:14 says, "Listen to this, O Job; stand still and consider the wonders of God." To be still and consider is a practice the Bible commends elsewhere, for instance in Exodus 14:13. The believer today may look at a storm, a snowfall or a night sky, and take it as a call to worship without treating it as a code. And Elihu's warning in Job 36:21, "Be careful not to turn to iniquity, for this you have preferred to affliction," should be read as a caution against choosing sin to escape pain, which is a real temptation for the suffering, and not as proof that Job had done so.

debates.question: Does Elihu's storm blend into the LORD's whirlwind?

views.label: Yes, a real storm arrives
views.case: Elihu says that his heart pounds at the thunder, that the tempest comes from its chamber and that lightning is loosed beneath the whole sky, Job 37:1-4 and 37:9. When the LORD answers Job out of the whirlwind in Job 38:1, it reads naturally as the storm Elihu describes becoming the vehicle of God's own voice. Many readers picture a storm gathering as he speaks.

views.label: No, the whirlwind is a separate event
views.case: The Hebrew words for the whirlwind in Job 38:1 and for the tempest in Job 37:9 are not the same, and the text never says a storm is visible before God speaks. Elihu's speech can be a poem about storms in general, and the LORD's appearance is a new act, not a continuation.

debates.bearing: The text does not settle it. Either way the effect is the same: the reader passes from a description of God's voice in the thunder to that voice itself, and Elihu's poem becomes the doorway.

debates.question: How should Elihu's warning in Job 36:16-21 be read?

views.label: As a fair warning to a man in danger
views.case: Elihu reminds Job that God once brought him to a spacious place and a table full of richness, and warns him not to be lured by riches or to long for the night. That could be true care, since Job did long for the night in Job 3:3-6.

views.label: As a mistaken accusation
views.case: He says Job is laden with the judgment due the wicked, Job 36:17, and hints that he prefers iniquity to affliction, Job 36:21. Since the reader knows from Job 1:8 that Job was blameless, the warning assumes a guilt that the book does not accept.

debates.bearing: These verses are hard in Hebrew, and English versions differ, as the BSB footnote on Job 36:19 shows. It is safest to take the warning as Elihu's view of Job's danger, not as the book's verdict on Job.

study.originalLanguages:
Elihu's opening claim, "one perfect in knowledge is with you," Job 36:4, is bold in any language. The Hebrew word for perfect, tamim, means whole, complete, without defect. It is a word used of offerings without blemish and of people who are upright. Elihu applies it to knowledge, and then in Job 37:16 he applies the same idea to God, asking Job about the wonders of Him "who is perfect in knowledge." The wording of the two verses is close enough that Bible readers have heard a quiet check on Elihu's self-description, since only God is perfect in knowledge.

In Job 36:5 God "despises no one." The verb means to reject or spurn, and the same assurance is voiced in Psalm 22:24, where the LORD has not despised or detested the torment of the afflicted. The affirmation in Job 36:5 that God is mighty in strength and yet does not spurn anyone is a compact description of a strong God who is not a bully.

The phrase "opens their ears" runs through Elihu's speeches. In Job 33:16 God opens ears with warnings in the night, and in Job 36:10 and 36:15 He opens the ears of the afflicted to correction. The idea of an opened ear is used elsewhere for the servant who listens: Psalm 40:6 says, "my ears You have opened," and Isaiah 50:5 says, "The Lord GOD has opened My ears, and I have not been rebellious." To have one's ear opened is to be made ready to hear.

The word for affliction, ani, and the related oni, appear together in Job 36:15. The BSB reads it as "God rescues the afflicted by their affliction," and its footnote gives "in their affliction." The two readings are different: one says affliction is the means of rescue, the other that God rescues while the affliction lasts. Either way the verse turns suffering into a place where God works.

In Job 36:18 the word rendered "bribe" is kopher, the same word used for the ransom of Job 33:24 and Exodus 30:12. The BSB translates it in Job 36:18 as a "large bribe," and there it is a payment offered to buy off judgment, and Elihu warns Job that no such payment will help. The word is the same, and the sense turns on who pays and why.

The Hebrew of Job 36:29 speaks of the "pavilion" of God, a word for a booth or tent. Psalm 18:11 uses the same picture of storm clouds as a canopy around Him. Elihu pictures the thunder coming from a covering in which God is hidden. The point is that we hear Him without seeing Him.

The end of the storm passage in Job 37:13 gives three purposes, which the BSB compresses. The Hebrew sets out whether the weather comes for the rod, for His land, or for loving devotion. The word for rod, shevet, is the staff of discipline, used in 2 Samuel 7:14 for the rod of men, and the word for loving devotion is chesed, God's covenant kindness. So the same cloud can strike, water or bless. Elihu names chesed among the reasons for a thunderstorm, which is a bold thing to say.

Finally, the verb in Job 37:14, "stand still," calls Job to stop and take his place before the wonders of God. Elihu's word for wonders, niphlaot, is the word used for God's great acts in the exodus, and in Job 37:5 he says God does great things we cannot comprehend.

typology.type: The voice of God in the thunder, Job 37:2-5
typology.fulfillment: Elihu says to listen to the thunder of His voice. The Old Testament speaks of God's voice in the storm, at Sinai in Exodus 20:18-19 and in Psalm 29, and the people asked that God not speak to them lest they die. The New Testament shows a voice from heaven heard by the crowd at the temple in John 12:28-29, some of whom said it had thundered. In Christ the voice that once terrified is now the Word made flesh, John 1:14, who speaks near and not from a mountain of fire, Hebrews 12:18-25. The correspondence is real; the type falls short because thunder terrifies while the Son invites.

Elihu says the clouds swirl at God's direction, accomplishing all that He commands. In the Gospels Jesus stands in a boat, rebukes the wind and the sea, and they obey, Mark 4:39-41. The disciples' question, "Who is this?", is the question the storm poem raises. The escalation is that the God who commands weather from a distance now does it face to face, in a boat with frightened friends. The type is not a prophecy in words. It marks out the kind of authority that the Gospels show being exercised by Jesus, and Psalm 89:8-9 supplies the same picture of the LORD stilling the sea.

typology.type: God's coming from the north in golden splendor, Job 37:22
typology.fulfillment: Elihu says that out of the north God comes in golden splendor with awesome majesty. Ezekiel's vision begins with a whirlwind from the north, a great cloud and fire and brilliant light, Ezekiel 1:4. The vision of glory finds its fulfilment in Christ, whose face is described in Revelation 1:16 as like the sun shining at its brightest. On the mountain of transfiguration His face shone like the sun, Matthew 17:2. The correspondence is that the unbearable glory of God meets human eyes. The type falls short because Elihu says no one can gaze at it, Job 37:21, while the gospel says that we see the glory of God in the face of Christ, 2 Corinthians 4:6.

study.christ:
Job 36 and 37 lead to Christ through the storm. Elihu asks Job whether he understands how God dispatches the clouds or makes the lightning flash, Job 37:15, and whether he can spread out the skies like a mirror of bronze, Job 37:18. The implied answer is that no human can. Then, in the Gospels, one man is in a boat on the Sea of Galilee in a violent storm, and He gets up and rebukes the wind and the sea, and it is perfectly calm, Mark 4:39. The disciples are overwhelmed and ask, "Who is this, that even the wind and the sea obey Him?" Mark 4:41. The question makes sense only because they know their Scriptures: Psalm 89:8-9 says the LORD rules the raging sea, and Psalm 107:29 says He stills the storm. The one who does it is Jesus.

The chapter leads to Christ by the voice. Elihu says, "Listen closely to the thunder of His voice," Job 37:2, and "God thunders wondrously with His voice," Job 37:5. The New Testament says that in these last days God has spoken to us by His Son, Hebrews 1:1-2. The voice that came in fire and thunder at Sinai, so that the people begged not to hear it again, Exodus 20:19, is the voice that in Jesus says, "Come to Me," Matthew 11:28. Hebrews 12:18-24 makes the contrast explicit: you have not come to a mountain blazing with fire, but to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant.

The chapter leads to Christ by the confession that we cannot draw up a case before God. Elihu says, "Teach us what we should say to Him; we cannot draw up our case when our faces are in darkness," Job 37:19. Job's whole quest had been for a hearing. The gospel gives what Elihu says cannot be had, since through Christ we have access to the Father, Ephesians 2:18, and He is our advocate, 1 John 2:1. We do not approach with a case. We come with a mediator.

It also leads to Christ by one strange detail. Elihu says God despises no one, Job 36:5, and rescues the afflicted through their affliction, Job 36:15. Jesus is the afflicted One who was not despised in the end: Psalm 22:24 says the LORD did not despise the torment of the afflicted, and God raised Him. By His affliction the afflicted are rescued, Isaiah 53:4-5.

A caution belongs here as well. Elihu's hymn is not a hidden prophecy of the Gospels, and it would be wrong to treat every cloud as a picture of the cross. The links rest on what the New Testament itself does, applying the language of God's rule over the storm to Jesus, and on the book's own movement from human speech to the voice of the LORD.
study.god:
The God of these chapters is great beyond our knowledge. "Indeed, God is great, beyond our knowledge; the number of His years is unsearchable," Job 36:26. Elihu's hymn puts that greatness in front of Job's eyes, in a way the earlier arguments could not. God is the teacher no one can rival, Job 36:22, the ruler whom no one appoints or corrects, Job 36:23, and the One whose ways man can see only from afar, Job 36:25. Zophar had said something similar in Job 11:7-9, and Paul says it in Romans 11:33.

God is the Creator who governs weather with a purpose. He draws up drops of water and distils the rain, Job 36:27, He commands the snow to fall, Job 37:6, He loads the clouds with moisture, Job 37:11, and He forms ice by His breath, Job 37:10. Elihu insists that no part of the storm is loose. It swirls at His direction, accomplishing all that He commands, Job 37:12. That is a doctrine of providence: God is not a distant clockmaker but the One who speaks to snow and rain.

God's purposes hold together severity and kindness. The same storm may be for punishment, for His land or for loving devotion, Job 37:13. By the same weather He judges the nations and gives food in abundance, Job 36:31. The doctrine of God cannot be reduced to either judgment or blessing, and Elihu names the covenant word chesed among the reasons for lightning. This is worth pausing over, because it means we cannot read a single storm and tell which purpose is at work.

God is just and not partial. Job 37:23 ends the argument with, "In His justice and great righteousness He does not oppress." The word comes as a reassurance to Job. God's power is not the power of a tyrant. Job 37:24 adds that God is not partial to the wise in heart, which is a warning to every speaker in the book, including Elihu, that cleverness gives no special claim.

Holiness runs through the whole. No one can gaze at the sun when it is bright, Job 37:21, and how much less at the One who comes in golden splendor, Job 37:22. Elihu's conclusion is not despair but fear, in the biblical sense of reverence: Job 28:28 says the fear of the Lord is wisdom. Worship, then, begins with standing still, as Job 37:14 asks, and with letting God be God.

There is a tension to name. Elihu says the Almighty is beyond our reach, and yet he speaks confidently about His purposes. The LORD's speech will honour the first and correct the second. The God who cannot be searched out is the same God who speaks to Job by name.

crossReferences.note: The LORD asks about the storehouses of snow and hail, the path of the thunderbolt, and whether Job can command the clouds and send lightning on its way. These are Elihu's themes in Job 37, taken up in the first person. The link shows that Elihu prepares the ground, and that God's questions go further than Elihu's.

Zophar asks whether Job can fathom the deep things of God or discover the limits of the Almighty. Elihu's confession in Job 36:26 and 37:23 repeats the thought, that God is beyond our knowledge and reach. It is striking that the humility Zophar used as a rebuke becomes a hymn in Elihu's mouth.

Job asks whether his friends will speak wickedly on God's behalf. Elihu says in Job 36:2 that there is more to be said on God's behalf. The earlier warning still hangs over the later claim, and it shows the risk of any speaker who says he represents God.

The voice of the LORD is over the waters, breaks the cedars and shakes the wilderness, and in His temple all cry, "Glory!" The psalm turns the thunder of Job 37:2-5 into worship, and it shows that Elihu's hymn belongs to a wider tradition of praise.

The LORD parts the heavens, thunders from heaven and hurls lightning. The psalm gives a full picture of the God who commands the storm and also rescues His servant. It matches Job 36:29-32, where the thunder comes from God's pavilion and lightning obeys His command.

God sends His command to the earth, spreads snow like wool, scatters frost like ashes and sends His word to melt them. The psalm has the same idea as Job 37:6 and 37:10, that snow and ice are obedient to a spoken word.

At Sinai the people saw thunder and lightning and trembled, and they asked that God not speak to them. Elihu's fear in Job 37:1-5 and his statement that no one can draw up a case before God in Job 37:19 are of the same kind. The people's fear was answered by a mediator, first Moses and finally Christ.

Ezekiel sees a whirlwind coming from the north, a great cloud with fire flashing and brilliant light. It matches Elihu's picture in Job 37:22 of God coming out of the north in golden splendor, and shows how the storm became the pattern of a vision of glory.

Paul ends his argument about God's saving plan with a cry over the unsearchable depth of God's wisdom and knowledge. It is the New Testament form of Elihu's confession in Job 36:26 and 37:23, that God is great beyond our knowledge.

Jesus rebukes the wind and the sea and there is perfect calm, and the disciples ask who He is. The storm poem of Job 36 and 37 raises exactly that question about who commands the clouds and lightning. The Gospel answers by showing Jesus doing what Scripture reserves for God.

Believers have not come to a mountain blazing with fire, darkness and storm, but to Mount Zion and to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant. The fear that Elihu describes before the storm-God is real, and the passage shows how it is answered in Christ.

The fear of the Lord, that is wisdom. Elihu's final call to reverent fear in Job 37:24 reaches the same conclusion as the hymn to wisdom, and shows that his speech, for all its faults, ends on what the book counts as true wisdom.

study.oneStory:
The Bible opens with God speaking and things coming to be: light, sky, waters, land, and the ordering of them by a word, Genesis 1. Elihu's hymn is a poem of that same creating word still at work. God says to the snow, "Fall on the earth," Job 37:6, and the clouds whirl at His direction, Job 37:12. The world is not a machine that runs without Him. The rain that falls, the frost that freezes the waters and the lightning that lights the sky are His acts, and Elihu wants Job to look at them again.

The speech looks back to the fall by its confession of human limits. Adam and Eve reached for knowledge beyond what they were given, Genesis 3:5. Elihu concludes that God is not partial to the wise in heart, Job 37:24, and that the wise man's place is to fear. The whole book of Job is a long lesson in that difference between wanting to know as God knows and learning to trust the One who does.

It sets up the LORD's speeches and, beyond them, the way the Bible teaches trust in the face of mystery. The storm that Elihu describes reappears at Sinai, in the psalms and in Ezekiel's vision, and it reaches a summit in the Gospels, where Jesus rules the storm and where the darkness at His death shows the creation itself in distress, Mark 15:33. Job could not draw up a case. What Job needed was not a better argument but a mediator and an answer, and both come in Christ.

The New Testament also carries forward the tension between fear and welcome. The disciples fear more after the storm is stilled than during it, Mark 4:41, and yet Jesus says, "Why are you so afraid?" Mark 4:40. That is the shape of the whole story: awe that becomes trust.

In the new creation the storm is no longer a threat. The One who sits on the throne is surrounded by a rainbow, and lightning and thunder come from the throne, Revelation 4:3 and 4:5, but the sea before it is like glass, Revelation 4:6. There will be no more sea of chaos, Revelation 21:1, and the people of God will live in the light of His face. What Elihu could only look at from afar, in golden splendor from the north, the redeemed will see, and their fear will be joy.

sermon.title: Job: Rebuked in Suffering
sermon.why: Piper's sermon on Job 32:1-37:24 explicitly notes that 'toward the end of Elihu's speech a thunderstorm had gathered and filled him with awe,' observing that Elihu 'senses the approach of God in this storm' just before the LORD actually speaks out of the whirlwind, precisely the transition this chapter's nature hymn accomplishes.

quiz.q: How does Elihu's fourth speech differ in tone from his earlier speeches?

options.text: It shifts from confident argument about justice into an extended hymn of awe at God's power displayed in the weather.
options.note: Chapters 36:22-37:24 build an increasingly breathless description of a gathering storm rather than continuing direct argument.

options.text: It becomes far gentler and more comforting toward Job than before.
options.note: The tone shifts toward awe, though it remains challenging, questioning Job's ability to understand or command creation.

options.text: It abandons any discussion of God's justice entirely.
options.note: The speech opens by continuing to defend God's just, disciplining purposes, 36:5-15, before shifting to nature imagery.

options.text: It stays focused mainly on abstract argument, only briefly touching on nature imagery near the very end.
options.note: Close, but this understates just how extensively chapters 36:22-37:24 dwell on nature imagery, nearly half of Elihu's entire fourth speech.

quiz.q: What does Elihu's storm imagery in chapters 36-37 set up?

options.text: God's own appearance and speech to Job out of an actual whirlwind in chapter 38.
options.note: Job 38:1, 'the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind,' follows almost seamlessly from Elihu's building storm description.

options.text: A literal historical flood that destroys the region.
options.note: The storm imagery functions poetically and theologically, preparing for God's speech, not narrating a literal flood event.

options.text: The final restoration of Job's wealth.
options.note: Restoration comes later, in chapter 42, after God's speeches and Job's response.

options.text: A further extended argument from Elihu himself about God's justice, continuing the same line as before.
options.note: Close, since Elihu is still speaking, but the storm imagery specifically anticipates a different voice altogether, God's own appearance in chapter 38.

quiz.q: What does Elihu mean by describing the storm as sent in God's 'loving devotion,' 37:13?

options.text: Even fearsome displays of power, whether for punishment or blessing, flow from God's steadfast, purposeful covenant character.
options.note: This ties even terrifying weather events to God's chesed, His faithful, loving purposes, not arbitrary cruelty.

options.text: Storms are always evidence of God's anger alone.
options.note: The verse explicitly says storms serve 'whether for punishment or for His land,' both purposes, not anger alone.

options.text: Storms mainly display God's raw power, with less emphasis on His purposeful, loving character.
options.note: Close, power is certainly on display, but verse 13 specifically ties the storm's purpose to God's chesed, His loving devotion, not power alone.

options.text: God has no control over the weather.
options.note: The whole passage emphasizes God's direct command over every element of the storm.

quiz.q: How does this passage anticipate an episode in the Gospels?

options.text: It anticipates Jesus commanding the wind and sea, prompting His disciples to ask, 'who is this, that even wind and sea obey Him?'
options.note: Mark 4:39-41 records this scene, echoing exactly the kind of questions Elihu raises about who controls creation.

options.text: It anticipates the disciples calming a storm on their own.
options.note: In the Gospel account, Jesus, not the disciples, commands the storm to be still.

options.text: It anticipates John the Baptist's ministry in the wilderness.
options.note: The connection is to Christ's authority over creation, not to John the Baptist's ministry.

options.text: It connects loosely to Jesus' general authority over nature, without one specific matching Gospel scene.
options.note: Close, but Mark 4:39-41 is a remarkably specific parallel, not merely a loose or general connection.

quiz.q: What is the ambiguous status of Elihu at the end of his speeches, based on the book's later chapters?

options.text: He is neither rebuked alongside the three friends nor explicitly praised by God, leaving his exact standing deliberately unresolved.
options.note: God addresses Job directly in 38-41 and rebukes only Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar by name in 42:7-9, never mentioning Elihu either way.

options.text: God explicitly condemns Elihu as the worst speaker in the book.
options.note: Elihu is not named or condemned anywhere in God's speeches or the epilogue.

options.text: God explicitly praises Elihu above every other human speaker, including Job.
options.note: God's epilogue actually favors Job's speech over the friends'; Elihu receives no explicit commendation either.

options.text: God quietly endorses Elihu's theology by using similar creation imagery in His own speech.
options.note: Close, the tonal similarity is real, but God's speech never explicitly confirms or credits Elihu's specific arguments, leaving his status genuinely ambiguous rather than clearly endorsed.

questions: Elihu moves from argument to wonder as the storm builds. Is there an area of your life where shifting from trying to explain your suffering to simply standing in awe of God might bring more peace?
Elihu says even fearsome storms flow from God's loving devotion, whether for judgment or blessing. How do you hold together God's power and His love when life feels stormy?
Christ commands wind and waves with a word, the very authority Elihu says belongs to God alone. How does knowing Jesus holds this authority change how you bring your fears to Him?
Elihu's closing words describe men rightly fearing God because of His inaccessible greatness. What would a deeper, more reverent fear of God look like in your daily life this week?

Elihu is neither fully rebuked nor fully praised in this book, a genuinely mixed and complicated voice. Where do you need to hold space for someone's counsel being partly helpful and partly overreaching, rather than sorting people into simply right or simply wrong?

translationNotes.note: 'Among the male shrine prostitutes' refers to a class of temple functionaries associated with pagan fertility cults, used here as an image of a shamefully premature death among the godless.
'Whether for punishment or for His land' captures the dual purpose Elihu assigns to storms, both corrective judgment and life giving blessing, both flowing from the same divine chesed.

'Out of the north He comes in golden splendor' may allude to ancient Near Eastern associations of the north with divine dwelling, building anticipation for the LORD's actual approach and speech in the following chapter.
